analysis.one_liner: Bars health insurers and employers from discriminating based on genetic test results.
analysis.headline: The bill drew 164 House cosponsors, including 15 Republicans, but never received a hearing or a vote in any of its three committees before the Congress ended in January 2001.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would prohibit health insurers from denying coverage, charging higher premiums, or demanding genetic tests because of a person's genetic information or family medical history. It would apply to employer plans, individual insurance, and Medicare supplement (Medigap) policies, and would let states adopt stronger protections. A second title would make it illegal for employers, employment agencies, unions, and training programs to hire, fire, or classify workers based on genetic information, and would bar employers from demanding workers' genetic test results.
analysis.who_benefits: Anyone with a family history of a genetic disease, anyone considering a genetic test, and their relatives. The bill's protections were designed to let people take advantage of the emerging science of genetic testing without fear that the results would cost them their health coverage or their job.
analysis.who_benefits_short: People with genetic disease risks in their families

how_it_helps.text: Health insurers could not deny enrollment to a group, adjust premiums, or set individual-market eligibility rules based on predictive genetic information, including tests of family members and family history of disease.

Insurers and group health plans could not request or require anyone to take a genetic test, and could not collect, purchase, or disclose predictive genetic information except in narrow cases such as paying a specific claim or with the person's written authorization.
The same rules applied to Medicare supplemental (Medigap) policies and to state and local government plans, closing common escape routes.

Employers, employment agencies, labor organizations, and apprenticeship programs could not discriminate in hiring, firing, pay, or membership based on predictive genetic information, and could not request or require genetic tests except for workplace-toxin monitoring with the employee's written consent or voluntary services whose results only the employee receives.

Workers could sue in federal or state court, the Equal Employment Opportunity Commission would enforce the employment title with the same powers it has under the Civil Rights Act, and courts could award attorney's fees and expert costs.
States could keep or pass stronger genetic-privacy and antidiscrimination laws; the bill explicitly would not override them.

analysis.who_pays: Health insurers would lose the ability to use genetic test results and family history as an underwriting tool, which could raise costs for plans that end up covering people they would previously have priced or screened out. Employers would lose a (then-rare but legal) way to screen workers and would carry record-keeping duties for any genetic information they hold.

drawbacks.text: Blocking insurers from using predictive genetic information removes a cost-spreading tool: people who privately learn they carry a serious mutation could buy coverage knowing the risk is shared across the whole pool, which pushes premiums up for everyone rather than onto the people with the risk.

The bill covers health insurance and employment only. It does not restrict life insurers, disability insurers, or long-term-care insurers, the three markets where genetic test results could still legally be used against a person.

It leaves carve-outs: insurers may still request predictive genetic information to pay a claim, and employers may conduct genetic monitoring of workers exposed to toxic substances, which keeps some channels for the information to enter insurers' and employers' hands.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For most people the benefits outweigh the costs. The point of the bill was to keep fear of discrimination from deterring people from genetic testing and counseling at exactly the moment the Human Genome Project was making such tests common — a public-health rationale its supporters emphasized. The cost is genuinely borne by insurers and employers in the form of lost underwriting information and compliance duties, and it is real that pooled premiums could rise somewhat. The biggest honest criticism is scope: leaving life, disability, and long-term-care insurance untouched means the strongest financial incentives to avoid a genetic test survived this bill.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to three House committees the day it was introduced, then routed to subcommittees, and none of them ever brought it up for a vote before the 106th Congress ended in January 2001.

narrative.text: Rep. Louise Slaughter introduced the bill on July 1, 1999.
It was referred that day to the Commerce Committee and also to Ways and Means and Education and the Workforce — a multi-committee referral that gave each panel jurisdiction over part of it.

In July and August 1999 it was referred to three subcommittees: Commerce's Health and Environment Subcommittee, Ways and Means' Health Subcommittee, and Education and the Workforce's Employer-Employee Relations Subcommittee.
No hearing, markup, or floor vote followed; the only later activity was another statement by the sponsor in the record on July 20, 2000.
By the time the Congress ended on January 3, 2001, the bill had 164 cosponsors — 148 Democrats, 15 Republicans, and 1 Independent — and had never advanced out of committee.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Health insurers and employers kept the legal ability to collect and act on genetic test results and family medical history. Everyone with a family history of genetic disease kept the risk that the information could cost them coverage or a job.

for.name: Rep. Louise Slaughter (D-NY)
for.role: Sponsor; only microbiologist and the only geneticist serving in Congress at the time
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill, gave introductory remarks on the floor, and recruited a large bipartisan cosponsor list; reintroduced attention with remarks a year later.

for.name: 164 House cosponsors
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill across both parties, the kind of support level that usually pressures committee chairs to schedule action.

against.name: Rep. Thomas Bliley (R-VA)
against.what_they_did: Received the referral of the bill on the day of introduction and never scheduled a markup or floor action for it in the 18 months that followed.

against.name: Rep. Bill Archer (R-TX)
against.role: Chair, House Ways and Means Committee
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled committee action on the health-insurance provisions referred to his panel.

against.name: Rep. William Goodling (R-PA)
against.role: Chair, House Education and the Workforce Committee
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled committee action on the employment-discrimination title referred to his panel.

against.name: Health insurance industry
against.what_they_did: Opposed the strongest versions of genetic nondiscrimination legislation during this era, arguing that insurers needed medical and genetic information to price coverage and that limits would raise premiums.

sides.party_line_note: Cosponsorship was overwhelmingly Democratic but included 15 Republicans and 1 Independent; the bill never reached a roll call, so no vote split exists.

industries.note: The bill would strip insurers of their ability to require genetic tests and to use test results and family history to deny or price coverage in the group, individual, and Medigap markets. Insurers' interest in keeping that information ran directly against people who could be priced out or denied coverage because of their genes.

The bill would bar employers from requesting or requiring workers' genetic tests and would expose them to lawsuits for genetic discrimination. Employers' ability to screen hiring and firing on genetic risk came at workers' privacy and job security.

By guaranteeing that test results could not be used against a patient by insurers or employers, the bill would remove the main reason people declined testing, expanding demand for genetic services. Its interest ran alongside patients' interest in using the new science.

The bill left these markets unregulated, so people who avoided health-insurance discrimination would still face genetic screening if they applied for life or long-term-care coverage — a gap that preserved those insurers' underwriting advantage and the incentive to withhold test results.
